content: Data collection for key population-specific indicators often cannot be achieved through routine program monitoring alone; surveys are necessary to gather this information. For example, HIV care registers, pre-ART registers, ART registers, and PMTCT registers are used to monitor the implementation of recommendations, such as screening people living with HIV for TB symptoms at the time of HIV diagnosis and during every follow-up visit. Indicators to monitor the entire cascade of intensive case finding for TB can be found in the WHO TB/HIV Monitoring and Evaluation Guide (2015). Adjustments for age and sex may be applied where appropriate. These indicators indirectly measure the effectiveness of TB infection control measures in healthcare facilities. When implemented effectively, these measures can minimize exposure, reduce the risk of acquiring TB, and bring the relative risk of TB disease closer to 1. In many settings, routine program monitoring is insufficient to collect data on key populations, necessitating the use of surveys. For example, pre-ART and ART registers, as well as latent TB infection treatment registers (if available), can measure the completion rate of treatment for latent TB infection (LTBI) among people in HIV care. This indirectly assesses the effectiveness of adherence support mechanisms. Similarly, TB registers, TB treatment cards, pre-ART registers, and ART registers are used to evaluate the timeliness of ART initiation after TB diagnosis among people living with HIV, particularly those with profound immunosuppression. The percentage of healthcare facilities providing services for people living with HIV (including PMTCT) that have demonstrable TB infection control practices consistent with international guidelines is an important indicator. This is measured through supervisory visit reports or annual infection control surveys. These practices should be implemented in all healthcare facilities in countries with generalized HIV epidemics and at least in HIV and TB care facilities in countries with low-level or concentrated HIV epidemics. HIV-related comorbidities, both infectious and noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), are increasingly observed as the number of people on ART grows and detection improves. In lowand middle-income settings, TB, severe bacterial infections, and other opportunistic infections (OIs) remain the leading causes of HIV-associated morbidity and mortality across all age groups. Approximately 6 million people aged 50 years and older are living with HIV, accounting for 10% of all adults with HIV. Compared to their HIV-uninfected peers, people living with HIV are at higher risk of NCDs, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and certain cancers, as they live longer on ART and face compounded risks from aging and chronic conditions associated with HIV infection. Mental health disorders are also more prevalent among people living with HIV than in the general population. Children and adolescents living with HIV are similarly affected by comorbidities, with long-term effects of HIV or ARV toxicity leading to poor growth, stunting, delayed development, and chronic lung disease. In high-income countries, the pattern of comorbidities in adults has shifted with increased ART use, with chronic liver disease due to hepatitis B and C, cardiovascular disease, and non-AIDS malignancies becoming more prominent. In lowand middle-income countries, as HIV-infected children and adolescents live longer due to ART, a similar profile of comorbidities is expected. Early and effective treatment for children may reduce risks of stunting and chronic lung disease but could increase the risk of ARV-related toxicity. Better longitudinal data are needed to understand these trends. Opportunistic infections, such as TB, severe bacterial infections, and other OIs, account for the majority of the fiveto nine-fold greater mortality in low-income settings compared to high-income areas. Prevention, care, and treatment services along the HIV cascade are critical, but late diagnosis of HIV, delayed treatment initiation, treatment failure, and poor ART adherence contribute to the burden of OIs. Except for TB, diagnoses of OIs are not routinely included in national monitoring and reporting systems. Cardiovascular disease and diabetes are increasing among people living with HIV due to factors such as chronic inflammation from HIV infection, side effects of certain ARV drugs, lifestyle factors (e.g., smoking), and aging. WHO aims to better understand HIV-NCD comorbidities to inform prevention and control strategies. Interventions are needed to reduce modifiable risk factors for NCDs, such as tobacco use, unhealthy diets, physical inactivity, and excessive salt and alcohol consumption. WHO, in collaboration with partners, will review how best to monitor and evaluate the impact of interventions to mitigate NCDs in people living with HIV. Certain cancers disproportionately affect people living with HIV compared to non-infected individuals of the same age. Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and cervical cancer are classified as AIDS-defining malignancies. ART reduces the risk and improves survival for Kaposi sarcoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma but does not lower the incidence of cervical cancer among HIV-infected individuals. The incidence of other cancers, such as Hodgkin lymphoma and anal cancer, has increased among HIV-infected individuals since the introduction of ART. The influence of ART on the risk of these cancers is not well understood. The aging of the HIV-infected population likely contributes to the increase in certain cancers, as cancer incidence generally rises with age in both HIV-infected and uninfected populations. Prevention, early diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up of cancer in people living with HIV should adhere to clinical best practice standards. WHO has issued guidelines on skin and oral manifestations in people with HIV, highlighting treatment recommendations. However, HIV program monitoring systems in many parts of the world do not capture data on HIV-related malignancies. Programs can utilize other data sources, such as cancer registries or vital registration systems, to assess the burden of AIDS-defining malignancies, particularly in high-burden settings. HIV can cause a range of mental health disorders, including encephalopathy, depression, mania, cognitive disorders, and dementia, often in combination. Mental disorders are frequently associated with substance use, such as recreational drugs and alcohol, which independently increase behaviors that risk HIV exposure. Certain ARV drugs, such as efavirenz, are associated with central nervous system side effects. Monitoring and evaluation of HIV-related mental health disorders would help determine their epidemiological patterns, assess needs, and respond appropriately. However, data on HIV-related mental health conditions are limited and are rarely included in routine monitoring and evaluation systems. HIV coinfection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and/or hepatitis C virus (HCV) is common, with an estimated 5–25% of the approximately 34 million HIV-infected individuals worldwide also having chronic HBV and/or HCV. The burden of HBV coinfection is greatest in lowand middle-income countries, particularly in Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. Data on HIV-HCV coinfection in Africa are particularly scarce, with many studies limited by small sample sizes, non-representative populations, and reliance on HCV antibody assays with high false-positive rates. Routine screening for HBV or HCV is not currently implemented in ART programs, nor is there guidance on routine screening strategies. WHO is developing guidelines that will include recommendations on screening. HIV coinfection increases the severity of HBV and HCV infections, raising the risk of death from cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality while reducing treatment response. Most data on HIV/hepatitis coinfection come from high-income settings, where liver disease is a leading cause of death in HIV-HBV coinfected individuals. However, there is no evidence to suggest differences in natural history or HCV treatment response in other regions or settings. ART is now a core component of the national health sector response to HIV. Monitoring progress in ART scale-up is critical to tracking the overall HIV prevention and treatment cascade. Indicators follow individuals living with HIV from treatment initiation or re-entry through key outcomes, such as retention on ART, treatment discontinuation, loss to follow-up, and death. Recent developments in ART include WHO’s 2013 revision of recommendations for earlier ART initiation, based on evidence of clinical benefits and reduced HIV transmission. Using the new criteria, an estimated 85% of all people living with HIV are eligible for ART.
